nameStory: Fragrant sumac gets its name from the pleasant, spicy-sweet aroma released when you crush its leaves between your fingers. Unlike some of its relatives with more questionable nicknames like 'skunk bush' or 'polecat bush' (referring to the musky scent some people detect), this sumac's fragrance is generally considered quite pleasant. The scientific name 'aromatica' confirms what your nose already knows!
description: Fragrant sumac is a low-growing, spreading shrub that typically reaches 3-6 feet tall and often wider than it is tall. This deciduous member of the cashew family forms dense, rounded clumps with many branching stems. Its compound leaves are made up of three leaflets, giving it a somewhat similar appearance to poison ivy at first glance, though the two are easily distinguished once you know what to look for. In fall, the entire shrub transforms into a blaze of orange, red, and yellow colors.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three-part compound leaves with the middle leaflet larger than the side ones, arranged alternately on stems. Crush a leaf and smell the pleasant, spicy-sweet fragrance that gives this plant its name. The leaflets have rounded teeth along their edges.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny yellow-green flowers appear in small, dense clusters before the leaves emerge in early spring. The clusters are only about 1-2 inches across and have a fuzzy, almost dusty appearance up close.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, fuzzy red berries about the size of peppercorns appear in summer, clustered tightly together. These drupes are quite hairy to the touch and persist into fall, providing food for birds.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading colonies through underground runners, creating dense thickets. The shrub is typically broader than it is tall, with multiple stems arising from the ground rather than a single trunk.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young stems are smooth and reddish-brown, while older bark becomes grayish and slightly rough. The bark has a pleasant smell when scratched or broken.

habitat: Fragrant sumac thrives in dry, well-drained soils and full sun to partial shade, often growing on rocky slopes, hillsides, and edge habitats. In New England, look for it in open woodlands, along forest edges, and in disturbed areas where it can spread freely. It's particularly common in areas with sandy or gravelly soils and is quite drought-tolerant once established.

seasonality.spring: Small clusters of yellow-green flowers appear before the leaves emerge, making this one of the earliest shrubs to bloom. The new leaves unfurl with a fresh, aromatic scent when crushed.
seasonality.summer: Fully leafed out with three-part compound leaves and developing small red berries. This is when the fragrant foliage is most lush and the aromatic oils are strongest.
seasonality.fall: Spectacular fall color ranges from bright yellow and orange to deep red. The fuzzy red berries are most noticeable now, persisting after leaves drop.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the shrub's spreading, multi-stemmed growth habit. Red berries may persist into winter, and the reddish-brown bark becomes more prominent.

funFact: Despite being called 'sumac,' fragrant sumac is more closely related to mangoes and cashews than to the Mediterranean spice sumac used in cooking - they're all members of the cashew family, which explains why some people can get mild skin reactions from handling the plants!
confusionNotes: The three-leaflet arrangement can make fragrant sumac look like poison ivy from a distance, but there's an easy way to tell them apart: poison ivy leaflets are pointed and smooth-edged, while fragrant sumac leaflets are rounded with toothed edges. Plus, fragrant sumac grows as an upright shrub, while poison ivy is usually a vine. Remember: 'Toothed edges and shrub form - fragrant sumac's the norm!'
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this native fragrant sumac with the invasive tree-of-heaven, which also has compound leaves but much larger ones with many more leaflets. Also, while all sumacs in our region are safe to touch (unlike poison sumac, which grows in swamps and isn't actually a true sumac), some people may experience mild skin sensitivity due to the cashew family connection.
compareHints: Fragrant sumac is much smaller and more spreading than its tall cousins like staghorn sumac, which can reach 15-25 feet. While staghorn sumac has large compound leaves with 11-31 leaflets arranged feather-like along a stem, fragrant sumac keeps it simple with just three leaflets per leaf. The red berry clusters of staghorn sumac are also much larger and more cone-shaped, while fragrant sumac produces small, tight clusters of tiny red berries.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Staghorn sumac is easily distinguished from its relatives by its distinctively fuzzy branches - smooth sumac has smooth branches (as the name suggests), while shining sumac has a winged stem between leaflets.
Shining sumac is much smaller than staghorn sumac and lacks its fuzzy branches, while smooth sumac has completely hairless stems and duller leaves.
Smooth sumac differs from staghorn sumac by its hairless twigs and stems, while staghorn feels velvety-fuzzy.
